forces.title: Industrial Waste Heat Recovery and Waste-to-Energy Integration
forces.description: The European Union's Heating and Cooling Strategy for 2026 promotes integrated local heat planning, emphasizing industrial waste heat recovery and the development of circular energy systems. This strategy encourages the integration of waste-to-energy, biomass cogeneration, residual industrial heat, and thermal storage into local heat networks. Such initiatives effectively convert local waste streams and byproducts into dispatchable heat and power, significantly strengthening energy sovereignty and contributing to the circular economy goals. This represents a substantial tailwind for waste management operators.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Retailers' CSR Driving Waste Reduction and Recycling Initiatives
forces.description: Irish retailers are increasingly prioritizing corporate social responsibility (CSR) linked to sustainable and environmentally friendly in-store activities. This includes adopting energy-efficient equipment, eliminating single-use plastics, and enhancing recycling facilities. Retailers are also collaborating with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to reduce significant food waste from Irish households, estimated at €1.2 billion annually. These proactive efforts by the retail sector aim to address decarbonization requirements, improve cost bases, and meet growing consumer and investor expectations for ethical trading, creating a tailwind for waste management.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Retail Convenience H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Emerging Demand for Desalination Technologies and Infrastructure
forces.description: There is an increasing evaluation of desalination links in various markets, particularly as industries explore direct use of nuclear heat and steam for process applications. This emerging interest in desalination, driven by the need for alternative water sources, signals a potential growth area for the Water Supply & Treatment sector. The development and deployment of desalination plants require significant capital investment and specialized expertise, presenting new opportunities for utilities and engineering firms involved in water treatment and supply infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Utilities Divesting Non-Core Water Operations for Portfolio Focus
forces.description: A structural shift is observed where utilities are exiting non-core businesses, including water operations, to sharpen their portfolio focus primarily on electric businesses. These divestitures are driven by strategies aimed at simplifying operating footprints in priority markets and strengthening balance sheets. While this trend leads to reduced exposure to the water sector for diversified utilities, it simultaneously creates opportunities for specialized water management companies or private capital firms to acquire these assets, potentially leading to consolidation or new pure-play entities.
forces.source_title: The New Rules of M&A in Power and Utilities

forces.title: Increasing Pressure on Drinking Water Supply from Climate Change and Population Growth
forces.description: The European infrastructure sector is facing emerging challenges in drinking water supply. This is primarily due to the combined pressures of population growth and climate change, which contribute to more frequent droughts across numerous regions. These factors necessitate essential investments in water infrastructure, posing a significant headwind for water utilities as they must adapt to dwindling sources and ensure reliable supply to a growing populace amidst changing climatic conditions. This requires proactive planning and substantial capital expenditure for water collection, treatment, and distribution.
forces.source_title: Construction Outlook 2026: Growth returns to the European construction sector

forces.title: EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) Driving Circularity
forces.description: The EU's Regulation 2025/40, the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), is a significant structural change aimed at cutting packaging waste, boosting recycling, and simplifying labels. Effective from August 2026, this regulation will mandate producers to alter their packaging ranges, impose plastic levies, and set recycling mandates. These measures meaningfully reshape the economics of packaging and create strong incentives for improved collection and recycling within the EU, acting as a powerful tailwind for the waste management and recycling sector, particularly for plastic waste.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Food and Drink Sector H2 2025 Insights and H1 2026 Outlook

forces.title: Significant Supply-Demand Gap for Recycled Plastics Projected
forces.description: Future scenarios for recycled plastic project a substantial 30% to 40% gap between demand and available supply by 2030 for plastic types such as PP and PE. This shortage is fueled by increasing regulatory pressure for recycled content and evolving consumer preferences for sustainable packaging. Consequently, brands and retailers face challenges in meeting sustainability commitments due to insufficient volumes and competitive pricing for recycled plastic, posing a significant headwind for the plastic recycling segment of waste management.
forces.source_title: Transforming Maintenance with Artificial Intelligence

forces.title: High Cost of Chemical Recycling Hindering Investment in Europe
forces.description: The economics of chemical recycling in Europe currently present a significant headwind, as the cost of recycling polyolefins via pyrolysis is more than twice that of producing virgin polyolefins. This high cost, coupled with limited financial headroom from virgin plastics and margin pressures, discourages meaningful investment by plastics companies. This hesitation impacts the scaling of advanced recycling methods and threatens the achievement of ambitious 2030 recycling targets set by regulations like the EU PPWR, creating a risk gap for circular economy goals.
forces.source_title: Transforming Maintenance with Artificial Intelligence

forces.title: Risk of Not Meeting 2030 Recycling Targets Due to Investment Stalls
forces.description: There is a significant risk that the plastics industry and customers may not achieve the 2030 recycling targets, particularly those set by the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR). This risk stems from market fundamentals for chemical recycling remaining unattractive, which raises the bar for investment while shortening the runway for scaling. Consequently, many companies are standing still on chemical recycling projects, driven by high costs and uncertainty regarding regulation implementation, jeopardizing the ambitious circularity goals for plastic waste in Europe.
forces.source_title: Transforming Maintenance with Artificial Intelligence

forces.title: Long Timeframe to Achieve Cost Parity for Chemical Recycling in Europe
forces.description: Achieving cost parity between chemically recycled polyolefins and virgin plastics in Europe is projected to take at least 20 to 30 years. This extended timeframe, requiring cumulative global capital expenditures of at least €400 billion, presents a substantial headwind for accelerated investment in chemical recycling. The long investment horizon and the need for significant capital premiums create a challenge for companies and investors, making it difficult to justify immediate, large-scale deployments without sustained policy support and favorable market shifts.
forces.source_title: Transforming Maintenance with Artificial Intelligence

forces.title: Waste Management Firms Expanding into Mechanical Recycling Operations
forces.description: A notable structural change in the waste management sector is the observed trend of waste management firms moving into mechanical recycling. This expansion indicates a strategic shift to capture more value across the waste processing chain and secure feedstock. This diversification by traditional waste management players into recycling operations suggests a maturing market where vertical integration or partnership across the value chain is becoming crucial. It also highlights an evolving competitive landscape with increased participation from established players in advanced recycling methods.
forces.source_title: Transforming Maintenance with Artificial Intelligence

forces.title: Growing Importance of Waste-to-Energy Due to Landfill Reduction
forces.description: Waste-to-energy systems are gaining increasing importance and becoming a primary final disposal method, particularly in the EU, due to the reduction of landfilling. These systems convert municipal, industrial, and organic waste into useful energy, addressing both waste management needs and increasing renewable energy supply. The trend is bolstered by policies such as landfill bans, export restrictions, feed-in tariffs, and carbon pricing, along with global urbanization and rising waste volumes. This creates a strong tailwind for the development and deployment of waste-to-energy infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Sustaining the Private Capital Opportunity in Climate

forces.title: Dwindling Landfill Capacity Exacerbated by Textile Waste Volume
forces.description: The rapid increase in textile waste, with 120 million metric tons discarded globally in 2024, is severely exacerbating the problem of dwindling landfill capacity. In the US, for example, landfills could reach capacity by 2038 at current rates. This headwind affects waste management systems globally, necessitating urgent investment in alternative disposal and recycling solutions. The situation is further complicated by the export of unsellable garments to developing regions, often ending up in massive, visible landfills abroad, highlighting a systemic global challenge.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: EU Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Regulations for Textile Waste
forces.description: New EU Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations are fundamentally reshaping textile waste management by shifting accountability for products' end-of-life onto producers. These structural changes require manufacturers to finance the collection and recycling efforts for their goods sold within the EU. This regulatory push is a direct response to textiles being among the top five household product categories contributing to climate change, creating a strong tailwind for the development of more robust and funded textile recycling infrastructures across Europe.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Expected Demand-Supply Gap for Recycled Textiles by 2030
forces.description: The textile industry faces a significant headwind with demand for recycled textiles projected to exceed supply by 30 to 40 million metric tons by 2030. This gap is driven by rising regulatory pressure for recycled content and growing brand investments in textile-to-textile recycling. However, existing infrastructure, high costs of recycled fibers, and technical limitations in processing blended fabrics currently hinder supply, creating a critical challenge that necessitates substantial investment in collection, sorting, and innovative recycling solutions to meet future demand.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Higher Cost of Recycled Textile Fibers Compared to Virgin Materials
forces.description: A significant headwind for scaling textile recycling is the economic disadvantage of recycled fibers. Recycled polyester, for example, can be more than twice as expensive as its virgin counterpart, and recycled cotton also commands a premium. This cost disparity stems from decades-old global supply chains optimized for virgin materials, along with subsidies and the unpriced environmental damage of new production. This economic barrier makes recycled materials less appealing for manufacturers and brands, hindering widespread adoption despite growing sustainability mandates and demand.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Inadequate Textile Waste Management Infrastructure for Current Volumes
forces.description: The current textile waste management infrastructure falls significantly short of handling the immense global volume of discarded clothing, estimated at 120 million metric tons annually. Existing collection channels are primarily designed for resale rather than recycling, and manual sorting processes are inefficient for categorizing textiles by recyclability, composition, and color. This inadequacy results in only about 7% of textile waste being available as feedstock for textile-to-textile recycling, presenting a major headwind for developing a circular textile economy.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Technical Limitations of Recycling Blended Textile Fabrics Hindering Scale
forces.description: A critical technical headwind in textile recycling is that most existing industrial solutions, primarily mechanical, can only handle single-material textiles. However, modern fabrics are predominantly made from blends of natural and synthetic materials. This mismatch between waste composition and recycling capabilities creates a significant challenge for processing the majority of textile waste. There is an urgent need for innovative solutions that can effectively handle a broader range of blended fabrics and deliver cost-competitive, high-quality recycled products at industrial scale.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Lack of Industrial-Scale Textile Recycling Solutions in Value Chain
forces.description: Textile recycling remains the least-developed stage in the textile value chain, characterized by a severe lack of industrial-scale solutions. This absence of effective recycling methods, coupled with insufficient investment in innovation, poses a major headwind for addressing the growing textile waste crisis. Scaling up recycling requires significant improvements in technology, infrastructure, and operational practices, along with strategic decisions about network establishment to maximize efficiency and commercial viability. Bridging this gap is crucial for a high-functioning circular ecosystem.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Dutch EPR Regulations Setting Ambitious Textile Reuse and Recycling Targets
forces.description: The Netherlands has introduced ambitious Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations for textiles, mandating that by 2030, companies must prepare 75% of textiles introduced to the Dutch market for reuse or recycling. Furthermore, at least 33% of fibers from discarded textiles must be incorporated into new textile-to-textile recycled products by the same year. These stringent requirements represent a significant structural change and a strong tailwind, driving investment and innovation in textile waste management, collection, and advanced recycling technologies within the Dutch market.
forces.source_title: Spinning Textile Waste into Value

forces.title: Global Water Demand Projected to Exceed Supply by 40% by 2030
forces.description: A critical key risk facing water utilities is the projection that global water demand will exceed supply by 40% by 2030. This imbalance is driven by climate change, rapid urbanization, inefficient water management, and unsustainable consumption patterns. This impending crisis necessitates urgent and transformative action across the entire water value chain, from sourcing and treatment to distribution and conservation, posing significant challenges for utilities to ensure sustainable access and manage resources effectively in the coming years.
forces.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

forces.title: Significant Water Losses by Utilities Due to Leakages and Unbilled Consumption
forces.description: Water utilities globally are experiencing substantial losses, with over 126 billion cubic meters of water annually lost due to leakages or unbilled consumption. This equates to nearly one-third of treated water for the average utility. These significant water losses represent a major headwind, impacting utilities' financial viability, limiting their ability to meet rising demand, and hindering the expansion of access to safe water. Addressing these inefficiencies through improved infrastructure and advanced management systems is crucial for sustainability.
forces.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

forces.title: Aging Infrastructure, Underinvestment, and Inefficient Water Management Hindering Utilities
forces.description: Water utilities globally are significantly hindered by aging infrastructure, chronic underinvestment, and pervasive inefficient management practices. These systemic issues severely limit their capacity to meet rapidly rising water demand, secure long-term financial viability, and effectively expand access to safe water services. This combination of factors creates a strong headwind, perpetuating a cycle of low service quality and insufficient revenue generation, which in turn stifles the creditworthiness required for vital infrastructure upgrades and operational enhancements.
forces.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

forces.title: Vicious Cycle of Low Service Quality and Insufficient Revenue for Water Utilities
forces.description: Many water utilities are trapped in a detrimental vicious cycle characterized by low service quality, declining customer trust, and insufficient revenue generation. This cycle significantly erodes their creditworthiness, making it exceedingly difficult to secure the necessary investments for enhancing service levels and expanding infrastructure. This fundamental key risk prevents utilities from breaking free from reactive crisis management, ultimately hindering their ability to transition to financially sustainable and scalable operations required to meet current and future water challenges.
forces.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

forces.title: Positive Consumer Engagement with Irish Deposit Return Scheme
forces.description: Ireland's deposit return scheme, launched in February 2024, has seen improving consumer engagement, with 900 million returns recorded by Re-Turn Ireland by the end of the year. This positive trend demonstrates growing public participation in packaging recycling efforts, suggesting that well-implemented schemes with accessible infrastructure and consumer incentives can effectively mobilize the public. This serves as a significant tailwind for the waste management sector, validating policy efforts to boost recycling rates and reduce packaging waste through public involvement.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Retail Convenience 2024 Insights / 2025 Outlook January 2025

forces.title: Delays in National Development Plan Impacting Irish Water Infrastructure
forces.description: Ireland's National Development Plan (NDP) is experiencing delays, coupled with planning issues and other rigidities, which are hindering the timely address of pressing infrastructural bottlenecks and capacity pressures, notably in housing and implicitly in related water infrastructure. This situation, highlighted by fluctuations in water infrastructure charges, poses a headwind for the Water Supply & Treatment sector in Ireland. Untimely resolution of these issues could impede necessary upgrades and expansion, affecting the ability to meet growing demands and ensure robust water services for the population.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sector Insights & Outlook February 2025

viewpoints.title: Irish Retailers Prioritizing Waste Reduction and Recycling for Sustainability Goals
viewpoints.description: Irish retailers are actively developing robust strategies for decarbonization, with a strong focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives. Key efforts include implementing energy-efficient equipment, eliminating single-use plastics, and enhancing in-store recycling facilities. They are also working with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to reduce food waste, estimated at €1.2 billion annually from Irish households, through education and portion size adjustments. This proactive approach aims to improve cost bases while meeting evolving government, investor, and consumer expectations for ethical and sustainable trading practices.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Retail Convenience H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

viewpoints.title: Ireland Lagging in Recycling Efforts Amidst Broader Sustainability Push
viewpoints.description: Despite strong performance in other sustainability metrics like low CO2 emissions and water stress, Ireland is currently trailing its European peers in recycling. This assessment, based on Allianz's proprietary Environmental Sustainability Index, highlights a critical area where the country needs to improve. While Irish retailers are actively engaged in waste reduction and recycling initiatives, the national performance suggests broader systemic improvements are required to align with leading economies and meet growing environmental mandates. Addressing this gap is essential for Ireland's overall sustainability profile.
viewpoints.source_title: 2026 Ireland country risks: Strong tailwinds set to persist amid strong buffers

viewpoints.title: Chemical Recycling Critical for Future Plastics Industry Leadership and Sustainability
viewpoints.description: Chemical recycling technologies, including gasification, pyrolysis, and glycolysis, are identified as fundamental for transforming plastic waste into new raw materials. Bain argues that these advanced methods are crucial for plastics firms to build sustainable long-term advantages, despite initial high costs and current economic hurdles. The firm emphasizes that delaying investment in chemical recycling risks ceding critical market positions to competitors, specialists, or even consumer goods companies, underscoring its pivotal role in the industry's future and the broader circular economy transition.

viewpoints.title: European Plastics Firms Hesitate on Chemical Recycling Investment Due to Unfavorable Economics
viewpoints.description: Most plastics companies in Europe are reluctant to make significant investments in chemical recycling, often backing away from previously announced plans. This hesitation stems primarily from unfavorable economics, where recycling polyolefins via pyrolysis currently costs more than twice as much as producing virgin polyolefins in Europe. This substantial cost gap, which is even wider in other regions, restricts chemical recycling to niche applications and highlights the need for policy intervention to bridge the financial viability gap and encourage necessary scaling.

viewpoints.title: Proactive and Strategic Investment Key to Chemical Recycling Advantage for Plastics Producers
viewpoints.description: Despite current economic challenges and market uncertainties, Bain asserts that early and strategic investment in chemical recycling is vital for plastics producers to gain a competitive edge. Winners in this nascent market are expected to move rapidly to secure access to low-cost, high-quality recycled feedstocks, develop waste sorting and processing capabilities, and forge partnerships with waste and consumer goods companies. This proactive approach allows firms to capitalize on profitable near-term applications and prepare for faster scaling as the market matures and policy support converges, building durable advantages.

viewpoints.title: EU Packaging Waste Regulation Mandates Overly Optimistic for 2030 Recycling Targets
viewpoints.description: Bain identifies the European Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) as a positive step for circularity, but expresses caution regarding its 2030 recycling mandates. The firm believes these targets rely on overly optimistic assumptions about the speed at which the industry can increase supply. This regulatory ambition, combined with unattractive market fundamentals and limited financial headroom from virgin plastics, creates a risk that many companies may stand still on chemical recycling, potentially hindering the achievement of the overall 2030 recycling goals.

viewpoints.title: Textile Waste Crisis Demands Urgent Circular Economy Transformation and Investment
viewpoints.description: The world faces a growing crisis of textile waste, with 120 million metric tons of clothing discarded globally in 2024, an amount sufficient to fill over 200 Olympic stadiums. BCG highlights that approximately 80% of this waste ends up in landfills or incinerators, leading to significant economic loss (estimated $150 billion in raw materials value annually) and severe environmental impact. Addressing this requires a fundamental transformation of the fashion industry into a truly circular economy, as current recycling systems are inadequate to handle the immense scale of textile output.

viewpoints.title: Significant Economic Value in Scaling Circular Textile Economy and Recycling
viewpoints.description: BCG projects substantial economic and employment benefits from establishing a large-scale circular textile economy. By surpassing 30% waste recycling rates, the industry could generate over $50 billion in new fiber raw material value and create approximately 180,000 new jobs. This vision, while requiring significant effort and investment across the value chain, represents a meaningful opportunity to reclaim lost resources and build a profitable, sustainable system for all stakeholders. It underscores the positive economic potential embedded in improved textile waste management.

viewpoints.title: Water Utilities Face Critical Challenges Amidst Global Scarcity and Inefficiency
viewpoints.description: Water utilities globally are at a critical juncture, confronting significant issues such as depleting water sources, increasing urban demand, and environmental challenges. Many utilities, particularly in emerging nations, struggle with aging infrastructure, inefficient operations, and financial constraints, which collectively hinder service expansion. The problem is exacerbated by substantial water losses due to leakages and unbilled consumption. This scenario necessitates a fundamental shift from reactive crisis management to proactive, data-driven operations, highlighting the urgent need for comprehensive transformation within the sector.
viewpoints.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

demand_drivers.description: Increasing landfill bans, especially in the EU, are making waste-to-energy systems the primary final disposal method.
Government policies like export restrictions, feed-in tariffs, and carbon pricing encourage waste-to-energy deployment.
Growing urban populations and increasing waste generation in emerging markets provide strong tailwinds.

new_opportunities.description: Opportunities exist to enhance existing waste-to-energy plants' operational efficiency and output.
Consolidation and regional expansion for waste collectors, sorters, and plant operators can create value.

market_sizing.methodology: Global market for systems converting municipal, industrial, and organic waste, and biomass into useful energy, including thermal conversion (incineration, gasification) and biological processes (anaerobic digestion).
market_sizing.source_title: Sustaining the Private Capital Opportunity in Climate

demand_drivers.description: EU regulations mandate recycled content and create incentives for improved collection and recycling.
Growing consumer demand for sustainable and non-plastic packaging options.

market_sizing.methodology: In 2023, approximately 40% of plastic waste in the European Union was recycled, with most undergoing mechanical recycling, often leading to downcycling.

demand_drivers.description: EU regulations are mandating higher recycled content in packaging, increasing demand.
Growing consumer willingness to pay a premium for recycled materials drives demand.

market_sizing.methodology: Future scenarios for recycled plastic predict a 30% to 40% gap between demand and available supply by 2030 for specific plastic types like PP and PE, driven by increased regulatory requirements and consumer demand for sustainable alternatives.

demand_drivers.description: Regulations like the PPWR aim to increase recycled material blending, though optimistic assumptions regarding supply need to be addressed.
Advancements in waste sorting, pre-treatment, and chemical processes will unlock cost efficiencies.

new_opportunities.description: Country-level or regional mandates could increase market penetration by 1-2% annually, leading to over 15% market share by 2040 and smooth capital requirements.

market_sizing.methodology: Achieving cost parity for chemically recycled polyolefins with marginal virgin plastic producers in Europe is estimated to require cumulative global capital expenditures of at least €400 billion. This includes an approximate cumulative cost premium of €270 billion borne by customers, regulatory mechanisms, and value chain margin investments. This tipping point is projected to take 20 to 30 years, contingent on virgin polyolefin prices, global adoption rates, technology advancements, and waste management economic models.

demand_drivers.description: Rising incomes, evolving trends, and changing consumer habits lead to more purchases and less frequent wear.
Current systems are not designed for the immense volume of textile waste, and collection channels prioritize resale over recycling.

market_sizing.methodology: In 2024, approximately 80% of discarded clothing globally ended up in landfills or incinerators. Only about 12% was reused, and substantially less than 1% was recycled into new textile fibers. This reflects a significant global waste problem where current systems are inadequate for the immense textile output.

demand_drivers.description: Lack of clarity on proper disposal methods for garments leads to mixed and contaminated waste streams.
Existing channels primarily support resale, not recycling, and manual sorting is inefficient for recycling needs.

market_sizing.methodology: Only about 7% of all textile waste generated is currently available as feedstock for textile-to-textile recycling. This low availability is a direct consequence of inadequate textile waste management infrastructure, including collection systems optimized for resale rather than recycling, and challenges in sorting mixed and contaminated waste streams effectively.

new_opportunities.description: Developing and integrating new collection strategies tailored to local factors like population density and existing infrastructure.

market_sizing.methodology: By combining new public and private initiatives with existing programs, the European Union could boost its textile waste collection rates by 20% to 25%. This effort aims to bring total collection rates up to 50% to 55% by 2033, addressing the current shortcomings in waste collection and making more feedstock available for textile-to-textile recycling initiatives.

demand_drivers.description: Altered weather patterns and increased droughts reduce available water resources.
Growing urban populations increase demand for water supply and treatment services.
Inefficient usage and consumption habits contribute to the overall demand exceeding supply.

market_sizing.methodology: By 2030, global water demand is projected to exceed supply by 40%, creating a severe crisis. This imbalance is primarily driven by climate change, rapid urbanization, inefficient water management practices, and unsustainable consumption patterns. This critical turning point in global water management necessitates urgent action and significant transformation within water utilities to ensure sustainable access.
market_sizing.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

pnl_drivers.description: Water lost through leaks in aging distribution infrastructure directly reduces revenue.
Water consumed but not accurately metered or billed results in revenue loss.
Suboptimal operational practices contribute to overall water losses and reduced financial performance.

market_sizing.methodology: The International Water Association estimates global financial losses from Non-Revenue Water (NRW) at USD 39 billion annually. These losses are attributed to leakages, unbilled consumption, aging infrastructure, and inefficient management, significantly impacting the financial viability and sustainability of water utilities worldwide.
market_sizing.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

pnl_drivers.description: Suboptimal processes in water production, distribution, and consumption lead to financial losses.
Impacts customer trust and willingness to pay, contributing to revenue shortfalls.
Inability to secure funding for infrastructure improvements exacerbates inefficiencies and losses.

market_sizing.methodology: The World Bank projects that a typical water utility loses USD 21.38 million annually due to various inefficiencies. These losses contribute to a vicious cycle of low service quality and insufficient revenue, undermining creditworthiness and hindering necessary investments for enhancing service levels and expanding access to safe water.
market_sizing.source_title: Digital Transformation for Growing Water Utilities

demand_drivers.description: Improved public participation in the deposit return scheme drives higher return volumes.
The introduction of the deposit return scheme provides a structured framework for recycling beverage containers.

market_sizing.methodology: By December 31, 2024, Ireland's deposit return scheme, "Re-Turn Ireland," recorded 900 million returns of beverage containers. Launched on February 1, 2024, the scheme initially faced mixed feedback but saw improved consumer engagement month-on-month, demonstrating growing public participation in packaging recycling efforts.
market_sizing.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Retail Convenience 2024 Insights / 2025 Outlook January 2025
